extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners in formalization, mechanized proof assistants, and philosophy of mathematics (Isabelle/Isar users, formalizers, proof-theorists)
extracted.subtask_description: Translating informal mathematical proofs into formal proof-language scripts (e.g., Isabelle/Isar), then evaluating those formalizations and the underlying inference methods with respect to readability, generality, and epistemic/methodological virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof as communicable text / readability
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof should be understandable as a communicable text; formal proof scripts should be closer to ordinary, informal proofs and emphasize assertions rather than purely operational instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Isar/Isabelle encourages writing proofs that make the assertions explicit and readable. The Isar tutorial advises: "Do not manipulate the proof state into a particular form by applying tactics but state the desired form explicitly and let the tactic verify from this form that the original goal follows." Readability correlates with robustness and with the formal proof's proximity to informal mathematical exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make implicit steps explicit for mechanization
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinary informal proofs contain large steps and vague instructions; formalization requires spelling out missing information (theorems, simplification rules, mechanisms) so that the computer can verify each inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate the proof into a formal language as straightforwardly as possible with the goal of mechanical verification; filling gaps reveals the background methods and resources needed to make the informal proof intelligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect and preserve definitions (do not auto-expand)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions should have a recognizable status and should not be expanded implicitly by the system; they are used to avoid repetition and to provide patterns for automated methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Isabelle never expands a definition unless explicitly instructed; treating definitions as first-class objects helps automated methods match tokens (like 'norm' or 'group') to relevant lemmas and tactics, and supports reuse and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declare appropriate lemmas and simplifications ([simp], [intro])
rubrics_metrics.description: Which lemmas are declared as simplifications or introduction rules affects automation and proof structure; the direction and presence of rewrite rules matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use annotations like [simp] to tell the simplifier which equalities to apply (often left-to-right). Be mindful: declaring permutative rules (e.g., commutativity) can cause infinite rewriting unless combined with conventions (e.g., left-commutativity) to enforce canonical ordering. Declaring or removing a simp/intro rule can make or break an automated proof; choose declarations to balance automation and transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control rewrite directions and canonicalization
rubrics_metrics.description: For identities without a preferred rewrite direction (distributivity, gauss-norm-mult, etc.), decide which direction(s) the simplifier should use and provide rules to canonicalize expressions (fixed term order and parenthesization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide conversion rules (e.g., left-commutativity) so nested operations are rewritten into a fixed order, preventing non-terminating permutative simplification and enabling pattern matching. Consider whether the reverse rewrite direction might be better as the default in some contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate proofs relative to background context and resources
rubrics_metrics.description: A formal proof script must be understood and evaluated with respect to the axiomatic system, standard and specialized libraries, available methods (lower- and higher-level), and other environmental resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because libraries and automated methods change, the assessment of a proof's simplicity, robustness, or naturalness depends on what is available in the proof environment. Provide explicit references to relevant library theorems and methods when evaluating or presenting proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generality and axiomatization of methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer methods and formalizations that are stated at the appropriate level of generality (e.g., axiomatic type classes like 'commutative ring') so proofs apply to broader classes of structures when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, axiomatize properties (rings, norms, etc.) so the same proof can be reused in more general settings; this supports understanding methods as instances of more general ones and facilitates reuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods should display constructive content / witness extraction
rubrics_metrics.description: A good method may do more than prove existence; it should show how to obtain explicit witnesses (e.g., instantiate metavariables ?x, ?y to concrete terms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Isabelle's facilities for unknowns (?x, ?y) to obtain instantiated terms; this provides additional information ("how" a problem is solved) beyond bare truth of the theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical effectiveness vs. blind completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods should be effective in particular contexts rather than relying on blind, systematic search which is generally impractical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek algorithms/methods that perform well in intended domains; characterize methods not only by theoretical completeness but by their practical utility and efficiency in the target proof states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterize and classify methods (taxonomy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop useful classifications of inference methods (algebraic, analytic, combinatorial, geometric, etc.) and identify method types used in particular branches of mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A taxonomy helps answer whether a result can be obtained by particular kinds of methods and aids comparative analysis across proofs and domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify methods required to understand a given proof
rubrics_metrics.description: For a concrete proof X, determine the set of low-level inference methods needed for a competent reader or system to recognize the proof as valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate proofs into formal representations to uncover the exact methods (lemmas, simplifications, rules) that make the informal proof intelligible; use comparative analysis to check generality and reuse of these methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze variation and interaction of methods across branches
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess how methods vary across branches of mathematics and how methods from different branches interact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate contexts in which collections of methods are useful and study cross-disciplinary transfers to understand methodological dependencies and synergies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate methodological / epistemic benefits of methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge methods by the epistemic and methodological benefits they provide: do they render proofs intelligible, show how to solve related problems, generalize to other contexts, or yield algorithms?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use criteria like intelligibility, generalizability, algorithm-extraction, and explanatory power when assessing the value of particular methods or method types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design proof-state and method models for evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a notion of proof state (local knowledge and subgoals) and treat methods as algorithms transforming proof states; evaluate methods by how they reduce epistemic requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A syntactic representation of proof states and algorithmic methods enables concrete evaluation of effectiveness, generality, and applicability; avoid overspecific representations but capture enough detail to compare methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Configure automation to use contextual clues
rubrics_metrics.description: Automated methods should be trained or configured to use contextual clues to choose fruitful rewrites and strategies, rather than applying global rules blindly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, provide context-sensitive heuristics or specialized methods so the automation better mimics human selective rewriting and avoids unhelpful expansions or rewrites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect and manage redundancy in formalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify redundant declarations/lemmas and manage them: some rules may be removable without affecting proofs, but removing multiple interacting declarations can break proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze which combinations of declarations are essential; prefer minimal, natural strategies but keep necessary helpers to avoid brittle formalizations.
